questions.subject: MATH
questions.learningObjective: Solve problems involving divisibility and primes.
questions.stem: In a practice quiz, 74 - How many positive divisors does 74 have?

options.misconception: it adds a phantom divisor
it counts only divisors up to the square root
it assumes every smaller number divides n

questions.explanation: Factor 74 and apply the divisor-counting rule: the number of positive divisors is the product of one more than each prime exponent, which gives 4. Choice B is a distractor: it adds a phantom divisor. Choice C is a distractor: it counts only divisors up to the square root. Choice D is a distractor: it assumes every smaller number divides n.
questions.hint: Use the prime factorization to count divisors.

it uses subtraction of the two numbers
it rounds up from the true divisor

questions.explanation: Applying the Euclidean algorithm to 169 and 103 yields a greatest common divisor of 1. Choice B is a distractor: it reports the least common multiple instead. Choice C is a distractor: it uses subtraction of the two numbers. Choice D is a distractor: it rounds up from the true divisor.
questions.hint: Use the Euclidean algorithm.

questions.stem: A textbook exercise: 21, 56 - What is the least common multiple of 21 and 56?

options.misconception: it multiplies without dividing by the gcd
it reports the greatest common divisor instead
it adds the first number unnecessarily

questions.explanation: The least common multiple equals the product divided by the greatest common divisor, so a b divided by gcd gives 168. Choice B is a distractor: it multiplies without dividing by the gcd. Choice C is a distractor: it reports the greatest common divisor instead. Choice D is a distractor: it adds the first number unnecessarily.
questions.hint: Use lcm(a,b) = a times b divided by gcd(a,b).
